subsection: 1. Emigration before and during the Famine, 1840–1855, and case study: Grosse Isle

notes.b: Emigration was already an established route out of Ireland before 1845, carried by networks of kin and by seasonal labour.
points: Ulster Presbyterians were the first large group of Irish emigrants to North America, sailing from the early 18th century to the American colonies.
Catholic emigration from the south and west grew in the decades before 1845, mainly to British North America (Canada), the United States and Britain.
Seasonal migration: labourers from the west and south crossed to England and Scotland each year for harvest work and then returned home.
By the 1840s Irish-born people made up a large share of the population of Liverpool, Glasgow and other industrial ports in Britain.
Liverpool was the main port of departure for emigrants crossing the Atlantic, with ships sailing from it to Quebec, New York and other North American ports.
Push factor: the subdivision of land into small holdings in the west and south left many families with plots too small to support them.
Push factor: heavy dependence on the potato for food left most of the population exposed to any failure of the crop.
Push factor: rent arrears led to evictions, which removed tenants who could not pay.
Pull factor: demand for labour on canal, road and railway construction and in expanding North American cities drew Irish workers abroad.
Pull factor: letters from earlier emigrants, describing land and jobs abroad, encouraged others to follow.
Pull factor: ships returning from Quebec to Britain and Ireland with timber took emigrants as cheap passengers.

notes.b: The potato blight of 1845 and the failures that followed turned a steady flow of emigrants into mass emigration.
points: The potato blight, caused by the water mould Phytophthora infestans, destroyed much of the potato crop in 1845 and again in 1846.
Blight returned in 1848, and 1847 was the worst year of the Famine, remembered as Black ‘47 for its heavy deaths and fever.
The 1841 census recorded about 8.2 million people in Ireland; the 1851 census recorded about 6.5 million.
The fall in population came from both deaths and emigration; deaths from famine and disease are generally estimated at about one million, though estimates vary.
Most estimates put emigration during the Famine decade at over one million people.
The poorest tenants and labourers, who had the least land to fall back on, made up a large share of the Famine emigrants.
Typhus, dysentery and cholera spread among the population at home as well as on board ships; a cholera epidemic struck in 1849.
Public works were started in 1846 as relief, but the schemes were criticised for slow pay and heavy labour that weakened starving workers.
Soup kitchens fed the destitute from 1847, and they were run alongside the public works until the government changed its approach.
The Poor Relief (Ireland) Act of 1847, known as the Gregory clause, denied outdoor relief to any tenant holding more than a quarter acre unless the tenant gave up the holding.
Tenants who surrendered their land to qualify for relief lost their homes, and evictions swelled the numbers who had to leave.
The Encumbered Estates Court, set up in 1849, sold indebted estates to new owners, who often evicted the tenants on them.
Some Poor Law unions and landlords paid passages for tenants, because sending people abroad was cheaper than supporting them on relief.

notes.b: Emigration in the Famine decade depended on money and tickets sent from abroad, which turned individual decisions into family and community movements.
points: Pre-paid passages: relatives or friends already in North America bought tickets and sent them home, so people who could not afford a fare could sail.
Chain-emigration: each emigrant helped others from the same parish or townland to follow, so the flow ran along existing networks.
Emigrants from the same district tended to settle in the same streets and neighbourhoods of cities abroad, where kin and neighbours could find lodgings and work.
Newspapers and letters from America and Canada circulated in Irish villages and carried news of wages, land and fares.
After 1847 many families were sent for in batches, so emigration often took whole households rather than single young adults.
Most Famine emigrants sailed from Liverpool or from Cork harbour, where Queenstown (now Cobh) was a major embarkation port.
Passengers in steerage were packed into the lower decks, where ventilation, water and food were poor.
Ships with high death rates from fever, hunger and exposure became known as coffin ships.
Typhus, called ship fever, spreads through lice in crowded conditions and killed many emigrants on passage.
Ships reached North America at Quebec, Saint John in New Brunswick, New York and Boston, and vessels with fever cases were held in quarantine.
Many emigrants arrived with no money or prospects, and some were dependent on charity in the ports of arrival.

notes.b: Grosse Isle was the quarantine station for ships arriving at Quebec, and it was the first point of arrival for many Famine emigrants.
points: Grosse Isle lies in the St Lawrence River, downstream from Quebec City.
The quarantine station opened in 1832 after a cholera epidemic, to inspect arriving ships and stop disease spreading into Quebec.
Medical officers boarded every ship, and vessels with sick passengers were held in quarantine while the sick were treated.
The island had sheds and hospital buildings where the sick were separated from the healthy passengers.
Quebec's authorities had planned the station for a small number of ships, and it was unprepared for the numbers that came in 1847.

notes.h: Case study: Grosse Isle, the 1847 season
notes.b: The 1847 season was the worst on the island, when ships queued in the river and fever filled the sheds.
points: In 1847 ships arrived in such numbers that they had to wait in a queue in the river for inspection.
Many ships carried passengers already ill with typhus, and some vessels were held for weeks while the sick were landed.
Dr Douglas, the island’s chief medical officer, was among the doctors who treated the sick, and his account became a central source on the season.
Doctors, nurses and priests who worked on the island caught fever, and several priests who tended the sick died of it.
About 5,000 people died in 1847 and were buried on the island, though figures differ between sources.
Children orphaned on the island were taken in by French-Canadian families in Quebec, many of whom raised them as their own.
Partridge Island, the quarantine station at Saint John in New Brunswick, faced a similar crisis in 1847.

notes.h: Case study: Grosse Isle, outcomes and memory
points: Grosse Isle became a symbol of the Famine emigration and of the suffering of those who reached North America.
A Celtic cross memorial was erected on the island in 1909 to commemorate the Irish dead.
The island and its memorial are now a national historic site in Canada, and they are visited as a place of Irish memory.
Contemporaries in Quebec struggled to find the money and staff to deal with the scale of the arrivals.
Irish nationalists later cited Grosse Isle as evidence of British neglect, while others pointed to the landlords who had forced tenants out.
Historians debate how far the British and colonial governments were responsible, and how far the crisis was beyond the capacity of any government.

notes.b: Judgements on Famine emigration turn on whether it is seen as relief or as a failure of policy.
points: Achievement: chain-emigration and pre-paid passages gave many Famine emigrants shelter, work and kin abroad, and so helped many survive.
Limit: the quarantine system could not stop disease, and the passage itself killed many people who had already been weakened by hunger.
Contemporary view: landlords and some officials welcomed assisted emigration as a way of clearing estates, while nationalists and tenant advocates condemned evictions that forced people out.
Later view: historians stress that British economic policy and landlord practice shaped who was forced to emigrate, and that the Famine was also a natural disaster.
Success and failure: emigration relieved pressure on the land at home, but the voyages and arrivals killed many of those who left.
